links.outcome: Proportion of LLM-cited PubMed references that were correct versus hallucinated
links.effect: 75% of referenced articles were properly cited from PubMed, 17% were hallucinations, and the remainder were not properly cited from PubMed.
links.quote: A total of 75% of the referenced articles were properly cited from PubMed, while 17% of the referenced articles were hallucinations, and the remaining were not properly cited from PubMed.

links.outcome: Clinician-rated correctness of RAG-grounded treatment recommendations and citation hallucination
links.effect: Clinicians labeled 25% of responses equal to their recommendations and 37.5% alternative plausible treatments, but 17% of references were still hallucinated despite retrieval grounding.
links.quote: Clinician-generated LLM queries achieved higher accuracy through clinician evaluation than automated queries, with clinicians labeling 25% of LLM responses as equal to their recommendations and 37.5% as alternative plausible treatments.

screen.reason: Evaluates a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline on retrospective molecular tumor board cases, measuring citation hallucination rates and comparing clinician-generated vs automated querying strategies with expert review.

primary.practice: retrieval augmented generation vs automated queries
